title: The Federalist Papers
author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay
openingText: After clear and unmistakable evidence that the existing federal government does not work, you are now called upon to deliberate on a new Constitution for the United States of America. The subject speaks for its own importance. Its consequences amount to nothing less than the survival of the UNION, the safety and welfare of its component parts, and the fate of an empire that is, in many respects, the most consequential in the world. It has often been said that the people of this country seem to have been chosen, by their conduct and example, to settle a critical question: whether human societies are truly capable of building good government from reflection and choice, or whether they are forever doomed to depend on accident and force for their political constitutions.
about:
In October 1787, three weeks after the Constitutional Convention sent the proposed Constitution to the states for ratification, the first of 85 newspaper columns appeared in New York under the pseudonym “Publius.” The Articles of Confederation had produced a national government that could not pay its debts, could not enforce its own laws, could not prevent states from fighting each other over trade, and had nearly collapsed during Shays’ Rebellion the year before. New York was fiercely opposed to ratification. Hamilton, Madison, and Jay wrote these papers to change that — quickly, in the columns of daily newspapers, arguing each objection as it arose.

They produced something they did not intend: the most important work of political theory ever written in America. The Supreme Court cites the Federalist Papers in major constitutional cases to this day. Madison’s argument in No. 10 — that a large republic neutralizes faction better than a small one, by multiplying competing interests until none can dominate — remains the analytic frame for understanding interest group politics, gerrymandering, and social media polarization. Hamilton’s argument in No. 78 that courts should have the power to strike down laws that violate the Constitution was written fifteen years before Marbury v. Madison made it a legal reality. The papers were journalism that became constitutional architecture.

whyItMatters.title: The most-cited work of American political theory
whyItMatters.text: Every generation of the Supreme Court reaches for the Federalist Papers when interpreting the Constitution. The papers are not just commentary on what the framers wrote — they are the clearest available account of what the framers thought they were doing. In landmark cases on executive power, the structure of Congress, judicial authority, and federalism, the Court treats Hamilton, Madison, and Jay as witnesses to original meaning. Reading them is reading the Constitution’s own explanation of itself.

whyItMatters.title: Madison’s faction theory still works
whyItMatters.text: Federalist No. 10 argues that faction — organized groups pursuing their own interest at the expense of the common good — cannot be eliminated without destroying liberty. The solution is structural: spread the republic across so many interests and factions that none can capture the whole. Madison’s analysis predates modern political science by 150 years, yet it precisely describes why social media algorithms, legislative gridlock, and polarization are so difficult to fix. The problem is not bad actors — it is the structure of incentives, and only structural changes can address it.

whyItMatters.title: Hamilton’s case for judicial review became reality
whyItMatters.text: Federalist No. 78 argues that courts must be able to strike down laws that violate the Constitution — that this is not a power grab by the judiciary but the only logical consequence of having a written constitution at all. The argument was controversial in 1788. Fifteen years later, Chief Justice John Marshall cited its logic in Marbury v. Madison and established judicial review as American law. Reading No. 78 lets you watch a constitutional doctrine being invented, argued from first principles, before it existed.

angleCards.title: The faction problem.
angleCards.text: Madison’s great insight in No. 10: faction is not a disease you can cure without killing the patient. Free people will always organize around interests, and those interests will always conflict with the public good. The solution is not moral reform — it is designing a republic large enough that no single faction can dominate. Read the papers asking: does the Constitution actually solve the faction problem, or only manage it?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Federalist Papers through the lens of Madison’s faction argument — tracing how the Constitution’s specific structures (bicameral legislature, separated powers, extended republic) are each designed to prevent any faction from capturing the whole, and asking whether that design has held.

angleCards.title: Checks and balances.
angleCards.text: No. 51 contains one of the most honest sentences in political philosophy: “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.” Madison is not appealing to the virtue of statesmen — he is designing a system that works even when everyone in it is self-interested. Each branch of government is given both the motive and the means to resist the others. Read asking how that design has held up across two centuries of strain.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Federalist Papers for their structural theory of government — how the separation of powers, bicameralism, and federalism are each designed to prevent the accumulation of power in any one place, and whether those mechanisms have functioned as Madison predicted.

angleCards.title: Judicial review.
angleCards.text: Hamilton’s argument in No. 78 is that an independent judiciary holding the Constitution above ordinary law is not a threat to democracy but its necessary guardian. Courts are the “least dangerous branch” — they hold neither sword nor purse. Read No. 78 alongside the history of Marbury v. Madison and ask whether Hamilton’s argument was right, or whether he underestimated what the judiciary would become.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Federalist Papers for Hamilton’s case for judicial review — understanding the argument that courts should have the power to strike down laws violating the Constitution, how he justified it in 1788, and what the subsequent history of American constitutional law suggests about whether he was right.

angleCards.title: Voice and authorship.
angleCards.text: Three very different men — Hamilton (combative, nationalist, former artillery captain), Madison (bookish, analytical, Virginia planter), Jay (diplomatic, reserved, eventual Chief Justice) — wrote as one “Publius.” They agreed on ratification but disagreed about almost everything else. Hamilton wanted a strong executive; Madison feared concentrated power. The scholarly dispute over which of them wrote certain papers lasted 200 years. Read asking what unified “Publius,” and what it costs an argument to suppress the disagreements inside it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Federalist Papers attending to voice and authorship — noticing where Hamilton’s nationalist urgency differs from Madison’s structural caution, understanding why they chose a unified pseudonym, and considering what the disputed papers (where scholars still disagree about authorship) reveal about the tensions inside the project.

cast.name: Alexander Hamilton
cast.description: Wrote 51 of the 85 papers — the most prolific contributor, and the most combative. A former artillery captain and Washington’s aide-de-camp, Hamilton believed a strong national government was not just useful but necessary for the republic’s survival. His papers on the executive (No. 69–77) and the judiciary (No. 78–83) are the most influential. He would later become the first Secretary of the Treasury — and be killed in a duel with Aaron Burr.

cast.name: James Madison
cast.description: Wrote approximately 29 papers, including the two most famous: No. 10 (on faction) and No. 51 (on checks and balances). A Virginia planter and constitutional scholar who had spent years studying historical republics before Philadelphia, Madison believed the Constitution’s structure was the answer to problems no moral appeal could solve. He would later serve as the fourth President — and become the figure most scholars credit with the Constitution’s design.

cast.name: John Jay
cast.description: Wrote only five papers (No. 2–5 and No. 64) before falling seriously ill. A diplomat and jurist who had negotiated the Treaty of Paris, Jay focused on foreign policy: why a united nation is less likely to provoke wars, less likely to be manipulated by foreign powers, and more likely to honor its treaties. He would become the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court.

cast.name: Publius
cast.description: The pseudonym Hamilton, Madison, and Jay shared — taken from Publius Valerius Publicola, one of the founders of the Roman Republic. The choice was strategic: a single authoritative voice rather than three men with visible disagreements. The fiction held well enough that scholars spent two centuries debating who wrote which papers. “Publius” argues for ratification with a consistency the three real authors did not always share in private.

cast.name: Faction
cast.description: Madison’s term of art, defined in No. 10: “a number of citizens, whether amounting to a majority or a minority of the whole, who are united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adverse to the rights of other citizens, or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community.” Faction is not synonymous with political party — it is organized self-interest that overrides the common good. Madison considered it inherent to liberty and therefore incurable by moral appeal alone.

cast.name: Checks and Balances
cast.description: The constitutional design principle that each branch of government — executive, legislative, judicial — holds both the motive and the means to resist encroachment by the others. Articulated most precisely in No. 51: “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.” Not a hope that statesmen will be virtuous, but an architecture that functions when they are not. The principle extends beyond the federal government to the relationship between federal and state authority.

preReadingChat.theme: Why are these called ‘The Federalist Papers’? Who’s Publius?
preReadingChat.response:
The name comes from the faction they were arguing for. In 1787, supporters of the proposed Constitution called themselves “Federalists” — advocates for a strong federal union — to distinguish themselves from “Antifederalists,” who feared the Constitution would destroy state sovereignty and individual liberty. The papers were written to argue the Federalist case, so the collection took that name when it was first published as a book in 1788.

Publius was the shared pseudonym chosen by Hamilton, Madison, and Jay. The name comes from Publius Valerius Publicola, one of the founders of the Roman Republic — a deliberately chosen historical echo, since the papers were arguing for a new republican founding. Writing as a single “Publius” had two practical advantages: it obscured authorship from political opponents, and it presented a unified voice when the three authors did not always agree in private.

The pseudonym worked well enough that scholars disputed authorship for two centuries. Hamilton left a list claiming most of the disputed papers for himself. Madison left a different list claiming them for himself. Statistical analysis of word choice and sentence structure has mostly settled in Madison’s favor for the disputed batch — but the dispute itself tells you something important: the three men wrote so consistently as “Publius” that even close readers couldn’t always tell them apart.

The papers appeared first in New York newspapers — the New York Packet and the Independent Journal — beginning October 1787, roughly one paper every few days. The pace was extraordinary: Hamilton wrote Federalist No. 51 through No. 85 in the space of a few months while also practicing law. These were not academic treatises written for posterity. They were political journalism written at newspaper speed, arguing a live controversy. That origin in urgency is visible throughout: the tone is direct, the arguments are practical, and the concessions to the opposition are strategic rather than academic.

preReadingChat.theme: What’s Madison’s faction argument in No. 10? Why is it still cited?
preReadingChat.response:
Madison opens No. 10 with a diagnosis: the great danger to republics throughout history has been faction — organized groups pursuing their own interest at the expense of the common good. His definition is precise: a faction is any group “united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adverse to the rights of other citizens, or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community.” This covers both majority factions (a majority using democratic power to oppress a minority) and minority factions (a powerful group capturing government against the majority’s interest).

The standard solutions, he argues, are both worse than the disease. You can cure faction by destroying liberty — since free people will always organize around competing interests, the only way to prevent faction is to prevent freedom. That’s no solution. Or you can try to make everyone hold the same opinions and interests — which is impossible so long as people have different faculties and circumstances. Faction is, as Madison puts it, “sown in the nature of man.”

So the solution cannot be to prevent faction; it must be to manage its effects. And here Madison makes his famous move: a large republic manages faction better than a small one. In a small republic, a majority faction can easily form, coordinate, and dominate. In a large republic spread across many states and interests, the sheer number of competing factions makes it unlikely that any one can achieve a national majority — and even if it does, the distance and diversity of the country makes it harder to coordinate long enough to act oppressively. Extend the sphere, multiply the interests, and tyranny becomes impractical.

This argument is still cited because it reframes the basic question of democratic design. The problem is not finding virtuous leaders — it is building structures that function even when leaders are self-interested. And the specific insight — that more interests and more diversity can be a feature rather than a bug — maps almost directly onto modern debates about gerrymandering (which shrinks effective diversity), legislative gridlock (which may be faction management working as designed), and social media filter bubbles (which reconstruct the small-republic problem online, where coordinating a passionate minority is suddenly cheap and fast). Madison wrote the analysis in 1787. The structure of the problem has not changed.

preReadingChat.theme: Is the original English hard to read? Should I use the modern edition?
preReadingChat.response:
The original English of the Federalist Papers is from 1787–88, and it reads like educated 18th-century prose: long periodic sentences, formal diction, Latin constructions, and a rhetorical style built for public declamation rather than silent reading. It is not impenetrable — these were newspaper columns written for a general literate audience, not academic treatises — but it does ask more of a modern reader than contemporary nonfiction.

The main difficulty is sentence length and structure. Hamilton especially tends toward sentences that run through several subordinate clauses before landing on the main point — the argument builds across the sentence rather than stating a claim and then supporting it. Madison is somewhat more compact. Jay is the most accessible. If you find yourself re-reading sentences to untangle the grammar rather than to deepen the argument, that’s a sign the original is costing you more than it’s giving you.

The modern English edition translates the prose into contemporary sentences while preserving the full argument. It uses shorter sentences and familiar constructions, which makes the logical structure — the actual political reasoning — easier to follow on a first read. The tradeoff is that you lose some of the rhetorical weight of the original: the cumulative pressure of Hamilton’s long sentences, the formal gravity that signals “this is a serious constitutional argument,” is part of what the papers were doing in 1787.

A practical approach: start with the modern edition to get the argument clearly, then dip into the original for the famous passages — the opening of No. 1, the key paragraphs of No. 10 and No. 51, Hamilton’s “least dangerous branch” passage in No. 78. Reading those in the original, once you know what they’re saying, gives you a feel for what made them powerful. The split-pane view in Tinct lets you hold both editions open side by side, which is probably the best of both options.

The Federalist Papers are 85 newspaper columns written between October 1787 and May 1788 by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay, arguing for ratification of the proposed Constitution. They were written in real time, responding to objections as they appeared — political journalism under a tight deadline. The result was accidental political philosophy: a sustained, systematic argument for republican government that the Supreme Court still treats as authoritative evidence of constitutional meaning.

The papers divide roughly by subject. Jay wrote on foreign policy (No. 2–5, 64). Madison wrote the most famous theoretical papers: No. 10 on faction and the extended republic, No. 51 on checks and balances and the design principle that “ambition must counteract ambition.” Hamilton wrote the majority of the papers, including detailed analyses of the Senate, the executive, and most influentially, the judiciary — No. 78’s argument for judicial review became the basis for Marbury v. Madison fifteen years later.

You don’t need to read all 85 in order. The most frequently read and cited are No. 10, No. 51, No. 78, and No. 1 (Hamilton’s introduction). Reading those four gives you the core arguments. The papers on specific constitutional provisions — the length of Senate terms, the treaty power, the structure of the House — are more useful as reference than as sequential reading. If a particular constitutional debate interests you, find the paper that addresses it directly and start there. The modern English edition makes the arguments easier to follow; the split-pane view lets you check the original at any moment.
